analysis.one_liner: Permanently bans offshore oil and gas drilling along the Atlantic coast and the Straits of Florida.
analysis.headline: The bill to permanently ban offshore drilling in four Atlantic planning areas was referred to the Senate Energy Committee in March 2023 and never received a hearing or vote before Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The COAST Anti-Drilling Act would amend the Outer Continental Shelf Lands Act to permanently prohibit the Interior Department from leasing or authorizing oil, gas, or mineral drilling in the North Atlantic, Mid-Atlantic, and South Atlantic planning areas and the Straits of Florida. Because a statute is much harder to reverse than a presidential policy, the bill would make coastal protection durable rather than dependent on whoever occupies the White House. It was introduced by Sen. Robert Menendez with 16 cosponsors, all Democrats or independents, and died in committee without ever getting a hearing or a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Coastal residents from Maine to Florida whose beaches, fisheries, and waterfront economies would be shielded from the risk of an oil spill, plus the tourism, recreational fishing, and commercial fishing businesses that depend on clean coastal waters. Under the bill, offshore wind and other activities could still be considered; only oil, gas, and mineral drilling would be barred.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Coastal communities, tourism and fishing businesses

how_it_helps.text: The bill makes the drilling ban permanent in law: the Interior Secretary could not issue any lease or authorization for exploration, development, or production of oil, gas, or minerals in the North Atlantic, Mid-Atlantic, South Atlantic, or Straits of Florida planning areas, overriding any other conflicting law.

Because the prohibition is written into the Outer Continental Shelf Lands Act rather than adopted by executive policy, it could not be reversed by a future administration the way a presidential leasing moratorium can — the protection would last until Congress itself changes the law.

By keeping drilling infrastructure off the Atlantic seaboard, the bill protects the beaches, fishing grounds, and coastal economies of states along the entire eastern seaboard and Florida from the risk of a spill and the industrialization of nearshore waters.

analysis.who_pays: Oil and gas companies lose potential access to Atlantic outer continental shelf areas, and the federal Treasury forgoes any future lease sale revenue and royalty income those areas might have produced. Consumers see no direct effect; the Atlantic currently has no active offshore oil production, and any output foregone here would be a small slice of national supply.
analysis.who_pays_short: Oil and gas drillers; federal lease revenue

drawbacks.text: The ban forecloses future domestic energy production and federal revenue: any oil and gas under the Atlantic would remain off-limits, and the Treasury would collect no lease bonuses or royalties from those areas, which critics of offshore restrictions generally cite as a cost to energy supply and taxpayers.

Restricting domestic leasing is sometimes argued to push supply toward imports or production in countries with weaker environmental standards, a tradeoff supporters of expanded drilling typically raise; the bill itself contains no offsetting energy provisions.
The bill is an all-or-nothing permanent prohibition rather than a managed-leasing framework, so if conditions changed it could be revisited only by another act of Congress.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is permanent, low-cost protection for a long coastline whose tourism and fishing economies depend on clean water, against the cost of foregoing potential Atlantic oil and gas development that does not currently exist and whose revenue would flow mostly to producers and the Treasury. The main honest cost is the loss of option value — future energy supply and federal royalties — but the asymmetry favors the ban: a single major spill would impose concentrated, lasting damage on coastal communities, while foregone Atlantic production would be marginal to national supply.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and sent to the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee in March 2023, and the committee never took it up before the Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Sen. Robert Menendez introduced the COAST Anti-Drilling Act on March 1, 2023, joined by 16 cosponsors — 14 of the Senate's 48 Democrats and 2 of its 4 independents — including senators from coastal states such as New Jersey, Rhode Island, Connecticut, Maryland, Delaware, California, and Oregon.
The same day, the bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Energy and Natural Resources, which is where authority over the Outer Continental Shelf Lands Act sits.

That referral was the final action of record: the committee never held a hearing, marked up the bill, or voted on it, and the full Senate never considered it before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, so the bill expired.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Oil and gas interests keep the legal possibility of future Atlantic leasing, since no statutory ban was enacted and coastal protection remains a matter of policy that can change with each administration. Coastal communities are left exactly where they started — protected only by whatever the sitting administration chooses.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Oil and gas interests; coastal protections stayed reversible

for.name: Robert Menendez
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on March 1, 2023 to permanently ban Atlantic offshore drilling.

for.name: 14 of 48 Senate Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including senators from coastal states such as New Jersey, Rhode Island, Connecticut, Maryland, Delaware, and Oregon.

against.name: Joe Manchin

against.what_they_did: His committee received the bill by referral on March 1, 2023 and never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: All 16 cosponsors were Democrats or independents and no Senate Republican signed on; the bill never reached a vote, so no roll call shows where opposition stood.

industries.note: The bill would permanently bar the industry from exploring, developing, or producing oil, gas, or minerals in four Atlantic planning areas, closing off future leasing opportunities. Its interest in opening those waters runs against coastal residents and tourism and fishing businesses that bear the spill risk.
Beach towns, charter boats, and shore businesses depend on unpolluted coastline, and a statutory drilling ban protects the beaches and waters they sell. The bill's name itself references tourism.
Drilling platforms, seismic surveying, and the risk of a spill threaten fish habitats and fishing grounds along the Atlantic; a permanent ban removes that threat.
